title: SYSK Selects: Bioluminescence: A Bright and Shiny Fish
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of the 2012 episode on bioluminescence. Josh introduces it as an original September 2012 episode. The hosts explain bioluminescence as cold light produced by a luciferin and luciferase reaction (versus incandescent bulbs), survey glowing organisms on land (fox fire, jack-o-lantern mushroom, fireflies, glow worms, some worms) and in the ocean (twilight/mesopelagic zone, blue-green light, loosejaw fish red light, tube worms, dinoflagellates and the milky sea, anglerfish). They cover theories on why organisms glow (communication, mating, lures, camouflage, counter-illumination, cookie cutter shark, defensive glowing clouds, burglar alarm theory) and an evolutionary theory that bioluminescence began as a byproduct of antioxidant activity (coelenterazine). They mention a glowing cat made by the Mayo Clinic using jellyfish genes (fluorescence, not bioluminescence). The back half is listener mail thanking listeners for gifts and cards.

segments.title: Selects intro and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh introduces this SYSK Selects episode as a September 2012 episode on how bioluminescence works. The hosts banter about foot massages on Buford Highway, fungus glowing, and Stone Mountain laser shows.

segments.title: What bioluminescence is
segments.summary: Incandescent bulbs make light by heating a filament, which is inefficient. Living things make cold light through a chemical reaction, similar to a glow stick, and scientists still don't fully understand many cases.

segments.title: Glowing organisms on land
segments.summary: Examples of land bioluminescence include fox fire fungus, the jack-o-lantern mushroom, fireflies (lightning bugs) and their larvae, glow worms, centipedes, millipedes, and worms that produce glowing sludge.

segments.title: The ocean twilight zone and blue-green light
segments.summary: The twilight (mesopelagic) zone, roughly 200 to 1,000 meters deep, is where most ocean bioluminescent organisms live. Light there is blue-green, and most animals produce light at a matching wavelength. The loosejaw fish can make red light.

segments.title: Why organisms glow: communication, prey, and dinoflagellates
segments.summary: Reasons for glowing include attracting mates, communicating, luring prey (anglerfish), and lighting the way. Dinoflagellates create the milky sea when disturbed, which the hosts relate to the Apollo 13 film and a burglar alarm theory.

segments.title: Camouflage, counterillumination, and defense
segments.summary: Some animals produce light on their undersides to blend with downwelling light. The cookie cutter shark glows with a dark spot resembling a small fish, then takes a round bite. Some shrimp release glowing clouds as a defense.

segments.title: The chemistry and evolution of bioluminescence
segments.summary: The reaction involves luciferin, the light-producing molecule, and luciferase, the enzyme catalyzing it, often with oxygen. The hosts discuss the etymology of Lucifer as 'lightbringer' and a theory that bioluminescence evolved from an antioxidant byproduct, with coelenterazine as an example.

segments.title: Glowing cats and fluorescence
segments.summary: The Mayo Clinic made a cat that glows green under blue light using jellyfish genes. The hosts note this is fluorescence rather than bioluminescence, since it reflects absorbed light.
